content: The reference lists of the reviews were meticulously examined to identify additional studies that could potentially meet the eligibility criteria. A comprehensive list of 137 articles, initially deemed potentially eligible but later excluded, along with the reasons for their exclusion, is detailed in Appendix 7. The process of study identification is visually represented in a flow diagram (Figure 1). To update the systematic review on indoor heat for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines, new searches were conducted in April 2018 to identify studies published since January 1, 2015. The original search strategies were applied to databases such as EMBASE (including Medline), Greenfile, Medline, PAIS, Science Citation Index, and Social Science Citation Index. The search strategies are detailed in Appendices 8–13. Two authors independently screened the retrieved records, and full texts were obtained for studies considered potentially eligible. Once obtained, the full texts were reviewed by two authors to ensure consistency. The flow of articles through this updating process is depicted in Figure 2. During the 2018 review update, the eligibility criteria were revised to include studies investigating the effects of indoor heat on health outcomes beyond those prioritized by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). This change aimed to broaden the scope of eligible studies and strengthen the evidence base for this section of the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. As a result, two studies from the 2015 search, which reported on non-prioritized health outcomes, were retroactively included. The updated review included no studies reporting on GDG-prioritized outcomes but incorporated two studies reporting on other outcomes. The updated search identified 6,669 records, of which 5,975 were screened after removing 694 duplicates. Following title and abstract screening, 7 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, with one excluded. Ultimately, six studies were included in the review, reporting on health outcomes not originally prioritized by the GDG. For eligible studies, data extraction and risk of bias assessment were conducted by one reviewer, with a second reviewer independently verifying the results for consistency. The accuracy of the extracted data and risk of bias assessments was confirmed through discussion. Extracted information included study location and date, study design, participant details, exposure and comparator specifics, relevant outcome results, and statistical adjustments for confounders. Risk of bias was assessed using criteria such as clarity of the study focus, acceptable cohort recruitment, accurate measurement of exposure and outcomes, identification and adjustment of confounders, completeness and duration of follow-up, reliability of results, applicability to the local population, and adequacy of statistical analysis and sample size description. The systematic review revealed a lack of evidence published after 2003 that directly links indoor temperature monitoring to prioritized health outcomes, such as all-cause mortality, heatstroke, hyperthermia, dehydration, or hospital admissions. This gap in evidence has been noted by other authors and limits the ability to develop evidence-based recommendations in this area. The Zero Carbon Hub reports also confirm this lack of evidence, discussing the effects of indoor temperature on health. Following the broadened eligibility criteria, eight studies were identified that investigated the effects of indoor heat on health outcomes, including sleep disorders (three studies), general health, blood pressure, respiratory and cardiovascular diseases (two studies each), body temperature, mental health, and pregnancy outcomes (one study each). A quasi-experimental study in the USA found that reducing the number of days above 27°C improved health and life quality, reduced emotional distress, and increased sleep hours. Three cohort studies explored the association between indoor heat and morbidity. One study in the USA found no association between indoor temperatures and respiratory viral infections or heat illness but identified a significant relationship between sleep problems and prior day’s temperature during summer. A Slovenian study reported worse cardiovascular symptoms with higher heat burden and poor indoor air quality. A case series in Korea and a cohort study in India found a non-significant positive relationship between indoor temperature and systolic blood pressure but a significant association with diastolic blood pressure. A case-control study in New York reported a non-significant increase in emergency calls for cardiovascular and respiratory distress with indoor heat above 26°C. A cross-sectional study in Ghana found a non-significant increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes with each 1°C rise in atmospheric heat exposure. The risk of bias assessment revealed mixed quality among the studies, with common methodological flaws including inadequate recruitment, failure to identify confounders, and insufficient sample size descriptions. For one study, only abstract data were available, making quality assessment challenging. An overview of the risk of bias assessment for each study is provided in Figure 3. Given the limited evidence on indoor heat and its direct effects on health, the review also considered studies that provided indirect insights. These studies highlighted the challenges in defining indoor heat thresholds for health and the variability in thermal stress among sub-populations and households. The ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 55 and other building standards were discussed as benchmarks for acceptable indoor thermal environments, though they are primarily based on working environments and may not address vulnerable populations adequately. In summary, the systematic review underscores the scarcity of evidence linking indoor heat to health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations such as the elderly. It highlights the need for more longitudinal studies and robust methodologies to establish evidence-based indoor temperature thresholds for health.
